project.name: Stone chimney — crack repair and stabilisation, upper section

overview:
Genesee Valley Stone Works has assessed the stone chimney at the above property following a site consultation. The chimney is a large historic stone stack rising roughly two storeys, with visible cracking through the mortar joints in the upper section and some stones that appear to have shifted. The chimney is no longer in service and is enclosed within the house interior; the objective of this work is structural stabilisation of the upper section, not restoration to working condition.

The masonry work itself is contained — the affected zone is the top few feet, with under ten linear feet of cracking. The governing constraint on this project is not the repair but the approach to it. The chimney is reached by a narrow, uneven, unpaved flagstone path of roughly three feet, on a wooded lot, and the work sits more than twenty feet above grade. A conventional self-propelled lift is very unlikely to fit that approach, and scaffolding is not workable for a single operator. Access equipment must therefore be specified and quoted before a committed price for the project can be issued. That figure is deliberately absent from this proposal rather than estimated, and Section 2 marks it accordingly.

materials_note: Material quantities in this table are estimates, not a take-off. Build date has NOT been confirmed. If the structure is pre-1930, lime mortar is a specification rather than a preference: Portland-based mortar is too hard for historic soft masonry and causes face spalling, so the repair visibly damages the thing it was meant to save. If it turns out to be later construction, the mortar spec and this line's rate both change. Stone matching on a historic stack is imperfect by nature; some visible variation should be expected and is not a defect. Material quantities below are estimates, not a take-off.

client_summary_para: Thanks for the time on site. Here's where things stand.

The repair itself is straightforward. The cracking is confined to the top few feet — under ten linear feet in total — and it's a mix of failed mortar joints and a few stones that look to have shifted. That's ordinary work on a stack of this age, and because the chimney is out of service, we're stabilising it rather than restoring it to function. That keeps the scope tight.

The complicated part is reaching it. The chimney sits over twenty feet up and the only approach is the narrow flagstone path along the side. That rules out scaffolding, and a conventional lift almost certainly will not fit; what should is a compact tracked machine that can travel a three-foot path without breaking your stonework. I'm getting that quoted this week and I'll come back to you with a firm number.
I've deliberately not guessed at that figure. It's the largest single cost in the job and I'd rather give you a real one a few days late than an invented one today.

One thing worth raising when we speak: because the chimney doesn't function and is enclosed inside the house, repairing it is a decision about how the house looks, not about how it works. There's a permanent alternative worth at least discussing before you spend money on access. Happy to talk it through either way.

integrity_flags.statement: Type N or NHL lime mortar is required on pre-1930 masonry. Portland-based mortar is too hard and causes face spalling on historic soft masonry — the repair damages the thing it repairs.
Rochester sees 100+ freeze-thaw cycles per year, the leading local cause of stone deterioration. An unheated, out-of-service stack has no thermal help at all.
If the top is being closed or crowned, hydraulic cement and waterproofing admix are required. Standard Type S will not hold on a water-shedding surface.

timing.hard_boundary: Masonry cannot be laid in freezing temperatures. NHL lime mortar cures more slowly than Portland and needs sustained above-freezing conditions.
timing.backwards_plan: On the wall by late October at the latest. That means access quotation and approval by early September, material ordering mid-September, allowing for a 1–2 week lead on lime mortar and any sourced stone.
timing.note: The seasonal boundary is real leverage and should be stated to the client plainly — not as pressure, as physics.

competitive_position.signal: Client is taking multiple bids and, per Dan, a number of masons are hesitant because of the access problem.
competitive_position.reading: Dan is not competing on price. He is competing on willingness — the field is thinning itself because of the very constraint that makes this job awkward. That inverts the usual pressure: the correct response is not to shave the number to win, it is to be the only bidder who arrives with a specific, credible method.
competitive_position.implication_for_this_document: The unpriced access line reads as a weakness only if the rest of the document is vague. Here it is surrounded by a named machine class, a measured site-visit plan, and a stated reason for the omission. Against competitors who are either declining outright or padding a number to cover their own uncertainty, a staged answer — site visit, equipment quote, firm price — reads as competence rather than evasion.
competitive_position.risk: The opposite failure is real too. A client collecting bids may read 'price to follow' as no bid at all. The covering note must make the sequence and the timeline explicit, so the gap looks like a process with a date on it rather than an open question.

access_scenario.provenance: Day rate recalled by Lindsey from Dan looking at a spider lift at Admar Supply, Rochester. Not obtained from the rental yard, not confirmed against a machine class or a working height.
access_scenario.days_note: 6 days on site — 1 delivery and siting, 3 masonry, 1 seal after cure, 1 strike and demobilise. Reconciled against the timeline in Section 4; the earlier 4-day model under-counted its own schedule.
access_scenario.weekly_basis: Rochester conventional boom rates: 60 ft at $640/day and $1,445/week — a multiple of 2.26 — per DOZR's published Rochester NY boom lift rates, retrieved July 2026. Spider lifts are a specialty class and may not follow the same multiple. Applying 2.26 to the recalled $680/day is an EXTRAPOLATION, not a quote.
access_scenario.headline: This job needs the lift for 6 days, not three. At the day rate that is $4,080. If Admar's weekly multiple resembles the local pattern, a week lands near $1,540 — roughly a third of the day-rate figure, a saving of about $2,540, and it covers the whole job with weather slack. Ask for the weekly rate first. It is the single largest saving available on this estimate.
access_scenario.not_included: Delivery and pickup, quoted separately and both ways. Damage waiver. These are the two lines that surprise people on specialty machines, and neither is modelled here.
access_scenario.validation: The tool named 'tracked / spider lift' from the memo alone — narrow unpaved path, landscaped surface, solo operator, 20+ ft. Dan had independently been looking at exactly that machine class at Admar. The reasoning arrived where the mason already was, which is the outcome to want: not a novel answer, the right one.

scenario_totals.caveat: Before sales tax, before delivery and pickup, before any change in the contingent masonry lines.

access_scenario.why_it_stays_internal: The client proposal keeps its blank. A remembered figure that reaches a client document becomes a number they hold Dan to, and the single most defensible thing about this bid is that Dan does not quote what he has not priced. The scenario exists so Dan can see the shape of the job — not so the client can.

call_sheet_priority: Ask for the WEEKLY rate first, not the day rate. This job needs the machine for about 6 days — $4,080 at $680/day. At Rochester weekly multiples a full week may land near $1,540. That single question is worth more than everything else on this sheet.

They are shown rather than left blank because the lift bills by the day, so the day count IS a price — these 6 on-site days are what turns a $2,040 assumption into a $4,080 one. cross_check.why: The rate card prices masonry per unit — per square foot, per linear foot, per stone. Those bands assume normal access and a mason working with a tender. This job has a small quantity of work and a large quantity of getting to it. So the two legitimate ways to price it disagree, and the tool surfaces the disagreement rather than silently picking the one it likes.

method_a.name: Unit price, off the rate card
method_a.note: Every line derived in Section 6. All-in per the card's Total Est. convention.

method_b.name: Day rate, off the card's quick reference
method_b.note: 6 on-site days — the same 6 the lift is modelled at in Section 7b — at the card's mason rate of $75–110/hr over 8-hour days, plus $590 materials. Solo working, so no tender rate applies. Siting and strike days are Dan's time too.

cross_check.gap: Unit pricing lands at $2,440. Day-rate pricing lands at $4,190–$5,870. The unit method is LOW by roughly $1,750–$3,430 — it does not merely differ from the day-rate method, it is under half of it at the top of the band.
cross_check.reading: This is not a rounding difference, it is the rate card telling on itself. Per-unit rates price PRODUCTION. On this job Dan is not mostly producing — he is positioning a machine, climbing, carrying stone one piece at a time, and repositioning. A small quantity in an awkward place costs day-rate money regardless of how few square feet it is.
cross_check.recommendation: Price this job on days, not units, and use the unit figure only as a floor. The rate card's own minimum-job clause ($350–600) exists for the same reason — it acknowledges that below a certain size, quantity stops predicting cost. This job is that case at a larger scale.
cross_check.instruction: Dan's call. The tool will not silently switch methods — it shows both and says which it would use.
